nameStory: This orchid gets its name from its delicate flowers that dangle on thin stems, resembling tiny crane flies hovering in the air. The scientific name 'discolor' refers to the leaf's two-toned appearance - green on top and striking purple underneath, making it literally 'two-colored.'
description: The crane-fly orchid is a woodland orchid with a unique two-season lifestyle that confuses many plant hunters. In fall and winter, you'll find a single oval leaf with a green top covered in dark purple spots and a brilliant purple underside. Come spring, the leaf disappears completely, and in mid-summer, a tall spike of tiny, delicate flowers emerges from what appears to be bare ground. The flowers are small and greenish-brown, dangling from thin stems like miniature insects.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Single oval leaf appears in September with green top often marked by dark purple spots and unmistakable bright purple underside that feels smooth and waxy to touch

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny greenish-brown flowers hang delicately from thin stems in July-August, each flower tilted slightly to one side like a small dancing insect

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows from underground potato-like corms in a distinctive two-phase cycle - leafy in fall/winter, then leafless flowering spike in summer

idTips.label: Seasonal Pattern
idTips.description: Leaf emerges in September and vanishes by late spring, followed by seemingly magical appearance of flower spike from bare ground in summer

habitat: Found in mature deciduous and mixed woodlands with rich, well-drained soil, often on slopes or in areas with good leaf litter. Prefers partial shade under oak, maple, and hickory trees. In New England, it's extremely rare with isolated populations, most likely in southern areas with milder winters.

seasonality.spring: The distinctive two-toned leaf begins to yellow and disappear by late spring, leaving no visible trace of the plant above ground.
seasonality.summer: Leafless flower spike emerges in July-August, reaching 1-2 feet tall with tiny dangling flowers that attract night-flying moths.
seasonality.fall: Single leaf emerges in September, displaying its characteristic green top with purple spots and brilliant purple underside.
seasonality.winter: The solitary leaf persists through winter, often one of the few green things visible on the forest floor, powered by energy stored in underground corms.

funFact: This orchid has evolved to trick moths into pollination by positioning its flowers at a slight angle so that when moths visit at night, the pollen packets stick directly to their compound eyes - essentially blinding the moth temporarily to ensure pollination!
confusionNotes: The purple-backed leaf might be confused with wild ginger or some trillium species, but crane-fly orchid always has just one leaf per plant and the purple underside is more vibrant than any other woodland plant. Remember: 'One leaf, two colors, orchid power!'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'crane-fly' orchid, it has nothing to do with actual crane flies - the name simply refers to the flower's resemblance to these delicate insects. This orchid is considered endangered or threatened in most states where it occurs, making any sighting in New England exceptionally special.
compareHints: As the only member of its genus in North America, crane-fly orchid is unique among New England orchids for its two-season growth pattern. While other woodland orchids like rattlesnake plantain also have distinctive leaves, none combine the purple underside, fall emergence, and summer disappearing act that makes crane-fly orchid so distinctive.
